title: Fatty Liver: Ayurvedic View, Causes, Tests, Diet & Lifestyle
excerpt: Has your ultrasound report said “fatty liver”? It is very common today and often grows silently without symptoms. Learn what fatty liver is, how Ayurveda understands it, its causes and tests, what to eat and avoid, daily routine and yoga, safe home measures and when you must see a doctor right away.
content:
Seeing “Fatty liver, Grade 1” suddenly written on an abdominal ultrasound, many people panic, and many others dismiss it as minor and forget it — neither is right. According to a large global study published in the journal Hepatology (Younossi and colleagues, 2016), about 1 in every 4 adults worldwide has non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD); in India too it is rising fast, especially among people with belly fat and diabetes.

The good news is that in the early stage, improving weight, diet and daily routine can reduce liver fat considerably. This article is for information only — take any treatment only on the advice of your vaidya or doctor.

What is fatty liver?

When more fat than needed builds up in the cells of the liver (yakrit), it is called fatty liver. Its main forms are:

  • Non-alcoholic fatty liver (NAFLD, new name MASLD) — the most common; linked to obesity, diabetes, high cholesterol and low physical activity
  • Alcohol-related fatty liver — from regular or heavy drinking
  • Inflammatory form (NASH/MASH) — when, along with fat, inflammation and damage begin in the liver; over a long time this can progress to fibrosis and cirrhosis

The ultrasound “grade” is only an estimate of the amount of fat, not of liver damage. So do not take Grade 1 lightly and do not panic at Grade 3 — what really matters is liver tests (LFT), assessing fibrosis and correcting the causes.

The Ayurvedic view

In Ayurveda the yakrit (liver) is considered an organ connected with blood. Describing the root of the channels that carry blood, Acharya Charaka says:

रक्तवहानां स्रोतसां यकृन्मूलं प्लीहा च ।
— Charaka Samhita, Vimana Sthana 5

Meaning: The roots of the channels that carry blood (raktavaha srotas) are the liver (yakrit) and the spleen (pleeha).

The name “fatty liver” is not found directly in the Ayurvedic texts, but the condition is understood as one of the santarpana-janya diseases (arising from over-nourishment), with an increase of meda dhatu (fat tissue) and of Kapha dosha; alcohol and spicy, sour and fried food also vitiate Pitta and blood. At the root there is often manda agni (weak digestion and metabolism). So the aim of treatment is — to correct agni, reduce the excess meda and Kapha, give up what burdens the liver, and exercise regularly.

Main causes and risk factors

  • Excess weight, especially fat around the belly and waist
  • Type 2 diabetes, prediabetes and insulin resistance
  • High triglycerides/cholesterol and high blood pressure
  • Sugar, refined flour (maida), sweet drinks, fried and packaged food; heavy meals late at night
  • Alcohol; and a sedentary lifestyle, too little sleep
  • Some medicines, hypothyroidism, PCOS and crash diets with very rapid weight loss

Symptoms and tests

  • Most people have no symptoms — it is found by chance in a report
  • Tiredness and heaviness
  • Mild heaviness or ache in the upper right part of the abdomen
  • Low appetite, indigestion, gas
  • A growing waistline and difficulty losing weight
  • Dark, thickened skin on the neck or armpits (a sign of insulin resistance)

Doctors usually order LFT (SGPT/ALT, SGOT/AST), an abdominal ultrasound, blood sugar and HbA1c, a lipid profile and thyroid tests. To assess liver stiffness (fibrosis), a FIB-4 score or FibroScan may be advised. Other causes such as hepatitis B/C are also ruled out by tests.

Diet: what to eat, what to avoid

In fatty liver the aim of diet is — to keep agni in balance, cut total calories and sugar, and lose weight gradually. According to Ayurveda, light, fresh, low-oil food and vegetables with bitter and astringent tastes are considered helpful in reducing meda and Kapha.

What to eat

  • Barley, bajra, jowar, ragi, dalia (broken wheat), moong dal — light food rich in fibre
  • Bottle gourd, ridge gourd, bitter gourd, pointed gourd, leafy greens, salad; half the plate as vegetables
  • Seasonal fruits such as papaya, guava, apple, jamun — in limited amounts, whole fruit instead of juice
  • Pulses, chana, buttermilk, a balanced amount of paneer/curd — for enough protein
  • Lukewarm water through the day; digestive spices like turmeric, cumin and dry ginger in food
  • A light dinner around sunset, 2–3 hours before sleep

What to avoid

  • Alcohol — in any amount
  • Sugar, sweets, cold drinks, packaged juices and sweet drinks high in fructose
  • Maida, fried food, namkeen, fast food, repeatedly heated oil and vanaspati
  • Frequent snacking, heavy late-night meals and overeating

Daily routine and lifestyle

  • At least 30–45 minutes of brisk walking or any exercise you enjoy, 5 days a week
  • Light weights or body-weight exercises 2–3 days a week, for the muscles
  • Lose weight gradually — losing even 7–10% of body weight is considered beneficial for the liver; avoid crash diets
  • Avoid daytime sleep; get 7–8 hours of sleep at night
  • Walk for 10–15 minutes after meals; do not sit continuously for long hours
  • Get sugar, lipids and LFT checked every 3–6 months as your doctor advises

Yoga and pranayama

Surya Namaskar (as per capacity), Bhujangasana, Dhanurasana, Ardha Matsyendrasana, Pavanamuktasana and Kapalbhati, Anulom-Vilom and Bhramari pranayama are considered helpful for digestion and metabolism. Caution: with high blood pressure, heart disease, hernia, recent surgery or pregnancy, avoid Kapalbhati and postures that press on the abdomen; learn yoga only from a trained teacher.

Safe home measures

  • Lukewarm water: the habit of drinking lukewarm water in the morning and through the day helps digestion
  • Turmeric in food: turmeric in daily cooking is fine; do not take high-dose capsules on your own
  • The plate rule: half the plate vegetables, a quarter dal/protein, a quarter grains
  • Instead of sweet drinks: buttermilk, lemon water (without sugar) or plain water

“Liver detox” drinks promoted on social media, living only on juice for days, or unknown powders can put an extra burden on the liver — avoid them.

Ayurvedic treatment — with caution

Ayurveda mentions many medicines for the liver and for meda-Kapha, such as — Bhumyamalaki, Kutki (Katuki), Punarnava, Guduchi (Giloy), Haridra (turmeric), Triphala, and classical formulations such as Arogyavardhini Vati. After examination, when suitable, shodhana (such as virechana), along with diet and lifestyle guidance and yoga and pranayama at the clinic, may be advised. But:

  • Which medicine, in what dose and for how long — the vaidya decides only after looking at the stage of the disease, age, prakriti, pulse, test reports and current medicines.
  • Do not stop your current medicines (such as for diabetes, cholesterol or BP) on your own; make any change only on your doctor’s advice.
  • Some herbs and untested “herbal” products can themselves harm the liver, so tell your vaidya the list of all your medicines, keep getting LFT checked during treatment as your doctor advises, and avoid “miracle liver tonics” without a name or address.
  • In pregnancy, breastfeeding, children and the elderly, any medicine only on the advice of a vaidya/doctor. Be wary of claims like “liver cleaned from the root”.

When to see a doctor immediately

  • Yellowing of the eyes or skin (jaundice), dark yellow urine
  • Vomiting blood or black, tar-like stools — go to hospital immediately
  • Fluid in the abdomen (swollen belly), swelling of the feet
  • Confusion, excessive sleepiness or a change in behaviour
  • Severe pain in the upper right abdomen with fever
  • Unexplained weight loss, marked weakness, or frequent bruising/easy bleeding

Summary — points to remember

  • Fatty liver is common and often has no symptoms — do not ignore the report
  • Gradual 7–10% weight loss, daily exercise and giving up sweet drinks are the most effective steps
  • No alcohol at all; cut down maida, fried food and heavy late-night meals
  • Keep diabetes, cholesterol and BP under control; keep up regular check-ups
  • Herbs and “detox” products only under the supervision of a qualified vaidya
